result: Forward genetics screen using ENU mutagenesis identified Kdm5a as a candidate ASD gene. The authors screened 350 G3 mice across 8 pedigrees carrying 409 mutations for defects in ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) and nest-building behavior. Automated meiotic mapping identified a single peak on chromosome 6 (p=2.9×10⁻⁵ for USV, p=7.0×10⁻⁵ for nesting) corresponding to a nonsense mutation in Kdm5a (p.C322*) that segregated with reduced USV peak frequency and impaired nest-building in a recessive manner.
evaluation: Claims C6-C33, C91-C93 provide comprehensive evidence for the forward genetics discovery. The screen design is well-described (C6, C15, C20-C27), the mapping results show statistically significant linkage (C31), and the identified mutation segregates with the phenotype (C8, C29-C30). The behavioral assays used (USVs and nest-building) are appropriately validated by citations (C16-C19). The scale of the screen (350 mice, 409 mutations) and the statistical approach (Linkage Analyzer with linear regression) are clearly documented. This represents the first successful identification of an ASD gene through forward genetics (C91), demonstrating the efficiency of this approach for heterogeneous disorders (C92-C93).

result: Generation and validation of Kdm5a constitutive knockout mice. The authors generated Kdm5a-/- mice using CRISPR/Cas9 to insert a single base pair in exon 13, predicted to cause a frameshift at codon 581. Western blot confirmed complete loss of KDM5A protein in knockout mice. Kdm5a-/- mice were viable, born in Mendelian ratios, and showed normal body weight, length, and brain-to-body weight ratio. The knockout mice replicated the Selbst phenotype with reduced USV peak frequency and an 84% reduction in USV number.
evaluation: Claims C37-C43 provide strong evidence for successful generation and validation of the knockout model. The CRISPR/Cas9 approach is clearly described (C37), protein loss is confirmed by western blot (C39), and the mice show normal viability and growth parameters (C40-C41). Critically, the knockout replicates the ENU-induced Selbst phenotype (C42-C43), providing genetic confirmation that loss of Kdm5a causes the observed behavioral deficits. The quantitative data (84% reduction in USV number) demonstrates a severe phenotype.

result: Kdm5a-/- mice display ASD-like repetitive behaviors, hyperactivity, anxiety, and social deficits. Knockout mice spent significantly more time in forepaw wringing/clasping and showed twice as much self-grooming compared to controls. In the open field test, Kdm5a-/- mice showed mild hyperactivity (increased distance traveled) and possible anxiety (less time in center). Social interaction was reduced by ~50% compared to control littermates.
evaluation: Claims C44-C48, C94 document multiple ASD-relevant behavioral phenotypes with quantitative measures. The forepaw wringing/clasping phenotype is particularly notable as it is characteristic of ASD mouse models and well-documented in Rett syndrome models (C94, supported by citation). The self-grooming increase (2-fold), social interaction deficit (50% reduction), and open field abnormalities are all quantified and statistically significant. However, the anxiety phenotype is appropriately qualified as "possible" (C47), suggesting additional validation may be needed.

result: Kdm5a-/- mice exhibit severe learning and memory deficits in the Morris water maze. Knockout mice showed impaired learning, with latency to reach the hidden platform not decreasing over the 4-day training period. Memory was also severely impaired, with knockout mice showing no preference for the target quadrant during the probe test.
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 provide clear evidence of cognitive dysfunction in Kdm5a-/- mice using the well-established Morris water maze test. Both the learning phase (C50) and memory probe test (C51) show severe deficits. The data presentation in Figure 2H-I shows appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA for training, comparison across genotypes for probe test). These findings are consistent with the role of KDM5A in regulating H3K4me3, a mark associated with memory formation and retrieval.

result: Loss of KDM5A causes severe neuronal morphology defects. Golgi-Cox staining and Sholl analysis revealed ~67% reduction in dendritic complexity, ~50% reduction in dendritic length, and ~33% reduction in dendritic spine density in cortical neurons from Kdm5a-/- mice compared to wild-type littermates.
evaluation: Claims C52-C54, C95-C96 provide strong quantitative evidence for neuronal morphology defects. The Sholl analysis is an appropriate method for assessing dendritic complexity, and the reductions are substantial and statistically significant. The findings are consistent with an essential role for KDM5A in dendritic morphogenesis and maturation (C95-C96), processes critical for neuronal circuitry establishment. The citation to Dong et al., 2015 (C96) appropriately supports the importance of these processes for brain development.

result: Identification of pathogenic KDM5A variants in nine patients with ASD. Through global collaboration, the authors identified nine individuals from seven families with pathogenic KDM5A variants (3 homozygous deletions, 3 homozygous recessive variants, 3 de novo heterozygous variants) that segregated with phenotype. All variants were absent from gnomAD (141,456 individuals), confirming rarity. Western blot and functional analyses demonstrated reduced KDM5A protein levels or truncated protein in affected individuals.
evaluation: Claims C59-C78 provide comprehensive evidence linking KDM5A mutations to human ASD. The identification of multiple unrelated families with different mutation types (deletions, splice site, missense, nonsense) strengthens the genetic evidence. Segregation analysis, absence from gnomAD, and functional validation (western blots showing reduced/truncated protein in C68, C70, C73, C75, C76) support pathogenicity. The CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in experiment for the KD-4 splice site mutation (C73) provides additional functional validation. However, some mutations are predictions (C33, C38, C78) that would benefit from additional functional characterization.

result: All nine patients with KDM5A mutations presented with ASD, complete lack of speech (or few words in one case), intellectual disability, and developmental delay, suggesting a role for KDM5A in regulating social communication in humans.
evaluation: Claims C65 and C103 document a consistent clinical phenotype across all identified patients. The complete absence of speech in all patients is particularly striking given the typical phenotypic variability in ASD, suggesting KDM5A may have a specific role in speech/communication. However, the inference about KDM5A's role in social communication (C103) is appropriately qualified as "suggesting" rather than definitively proven. The sample size (n=9) is relatively small for drawing broad conclusions about genotype-phenotype correlations.

result: Loss of KDM5A causes dysregulation of 450 genes in the hippocampus, with upregulated genes enriched in neurological processes and RNA splicing, and downregulated genes enriched in neurogenesis and cell proliferation. The most upregulated gene was Efcab6 (potential direct KDM5A target), and the most downregulated was Ptgds. Dysregulated genes included 15 ASD gene homologs and 33 genes essential for brain development. Shh and its target Ccnd1 were upregulated, suggesting a potential mechanism for KDM5A function in the hippocampus.
evaluation: Claims C80-C90, C114-C120 provide comprehensive transcriptomic analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR-corrected p≤0.05, log2 fold change ≥|0.3|). The RNA-seq quality metrics (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and clustering by genotype support data quality. The functional enrichment analysis identifies biologically relevant pathways, and qRT-PCR validation of top hits (Efcab6, Ptgds, Shh, Ccnd1) confirms the RNA-seq findings. The overlap with known ASD genes and neurodevelopmental genes strengthens biological relevance. The inference that upregulated genes are potential direct KDM5A targets (C114-C115) is logical given KDM5A's role as a repressor, though ChIP-seq would be needed for definitive identification of direct targets.

result: KDM5A is extremely intolerant to loss-of-function variation (pLI=1.00 in gnomAD), and prior to this study, it was unknown whether KDM5A mutations cause ASD. Only one recessive missense variant had been reported in association with an undefined developmental disorder. Other KDM5 family members (KDM5B, KDM5C) are disrupted in neurodevelopmental disorders.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 appropriately contextualize the novelty of the findings. The pLI score from gnomAD (C55) provides strong evidence for constraint against loss-of-function mutations in the general population. The statement about prior knowledge (C56) and the single previous report (C57) are appropriately cited. The information about other KDM5 family members (C58) provides important context for the biological plausibility of KDM5A involvement in neurodevelopmental disorders.

result: The neurobehavioral phenotypes in Kdm5a-/- mice recapitulate those in patients with KDM5A mutations. This is the first report implicating KDM5A disruption as a cause of ASD. The identification of both monoallelic and biallelic mutations, similar to other ASD genes (KDM5B, CHD8, DOCK8), emphasizes brain sensitivity to KDM5A levels. The nonredundant function of KDM5A, KDM5B, and KDM5C in the brain is indicated by the fact that mutations in all three cause neurodevelopmental disorders.
evaluation: Claims C97, C101-C102, C104-C109 provide appropriate synthesis and interpretation of the findings. The comparison between mouse and human phenotypes (C97) is supported by the data presented. The novelty claim (C101) appears justified given the literature review. The inference about brain sensitivity to KDM5A dosage (C109) is reasonable given both haploinsufficient and recessive mutations cause disease. The argument for nonredundancy of KDM5 family members (C102) is logical, though the lack of compensation by other family members (C84) provides additional support. The discussion of mutation mechanisms (C105-C108) appropriately cites structural and functional studies.

result: KDM5A is a histone lysine demethylase that removes methyl groups from H3K4me3, resulting in gene repression. H3K4me3 marks are present at promoters and active enhancers and are associated with memory formation and retrieval. Mutations in lysine demethylases regulating H3K4me3 are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders. Chromatin regulation is essential for gene expression and brain development, and mutations in chromatin remodelers have been linked to ASD.
evaluation: Claims C10-C13, C34, C79, C98-C113 provide appropriate background on KDM5A function and the role of chromatin regulation in neurodevelopment. These claims are well-supported by citations to the literature and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide important context for interpreting the experimental findings but do not constitute novel results from this study.

result: ASD is characterized by deficits in communication, social skills, and stereotyped behaviors. It is highly heritable, with thousands of genetic variations contributing to risk. Chromatin remodeling is a top pathway disrupted in ASD, but identified genes account for only ~30% of cases with no single gene contributing >2%.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide standard background information on ASD that is well-established in the field and appropriately cited. These claims contextualize the need for the study but do not represent novel findings. The citations to Colvert et al., 2015; Geschwind and State, 2015; De Rubeis et al., 2014; de la Torre-Ubieta et al., 2016; and Dias and Walsh, 2020 are appropriate.

result: Kdm5a is expressed ubiquitously in humans and mice, including in the brain.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 document Kdm5a expression patterns. The ubiquitous expression is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2019, and brain expression is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 using data from the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas. This provides important validation that the gene is expressed in the relevant tissue for the study.

result: The forward genetics approach underscores the value of this method for discovering gene defects causing phenotypically complex and genetically heterogeneous disorders.
evaluation: Claim C121 is a summary statement about the methodological contribution of the study. The successful identification of Kdm5a through forward genetics, confirmed by knockout validation and human genetics, supports this conclusion. However, this is a single example, and broader validation of the approach for ASD gene discovery would strengthen this claim.
